title: How to choose a video production company in Baltimore
description: What to look for before you book a crew, from finished work to how the team handles changes.
cta: Send us your goal, a reference you like, and your deadline. We can share relevant work and talk through what your shoot would take.
sections: Watch a whole video

A reel can tell you whether you like the look. Ask for a finished project that’s close to yours and watch it all the way through. Listen to how the interviews sound. Notice whether you understand the point of the film by the end. Ask what the crew actually handled on that job.
Ask who will be on the job

Find out who runs the shoot, who edits, and who will answer your questions after filming. If you need to coordinate executives, security or a busy venue, ask how the producer would schedule that day. Give them one real complication and see what they come back with.
Compare the same deliverables

Send each team the same brief. Ask for the number of shoot days, the length and format of each edit, the revision rounds, and the delivery date. A proposal that includes three finished cuts is a different scope from one that includes a single master.
Check the location and your own calendar

A local crew can still need time to load in, find a quiet room, and get approval to film. Share what you know about parking, room availability, and access. Pick the team that can explain how those details affect your day and your budget.

title: How to compare video production proposals
description: What to look for when two quotes describe the same project but come in at different prices.
cta: Get a quote you can compare
Send your brief and the deliverables you need. We can explain what goes into the estimate and where the scope can flex.
sections: Write down what you get at delivery

Put the final assets side by side. One quote might include a two-minute film and three social edits. Another might list “social deliverables” without saying how many or whether they’re edited separately. Get the quantities, lengths, and formats in writing.
Look at the assumptions behind shoot day

Ask which locations and hours the estimate covers, how many crew members are expected, and who provides talent, props, or access. If interviews are in two offices, ask whether travel and setup are included. The assumptions explain a lot of the difference.
Read the editing section carefully

Check whether captions, color, audio cleanup, music, and graphics are included. Ask when revision rounds begin and whether your team needs to send one set of notes. Agree on how added versions or changes to approved material will be quoted.
Ask for one alternate scope

If a proposal is over budget, ask the producer to show what they’d adjust. One location with a strong interview and planned supporting shots might get you to the same goal. A cheaper package makes sense when you can still see how it serves the brief.

title: What does a video production company do?
description: See what a production team handles before the shoot, on set, and after filming wraps.
cta: Figure out where you need help
Tell us what you already have, from a rough idea to footage in hand, and what you need delivered.
sections: Before filming

The producer turns the brief into a plan people can execute. That may include developing the idea, writing questions or a script, scouting locations, and figuring out how to get the right people into the room. You should know what you’ll be asked to approve before the crew arrives.
On set

The team manages camera, lighting, and sound while the director works with the people on screen. In a normal office, that can mean pausing for elevator noise or moving a setup so staff can keep working. A good schedule gives the crew room to handle those adjustments.
After the shoot

The editor finds the story in the footage, then builds a cut for review. Once the team approves the structure, the crew can finish color, sound, captions, and graphics. If there are different formats for web, social, or an event screen, each needs a final check.
Where the client comes in

Name a contact who can confirm access and one person who can consolidate feedback. Share brand files, names and titles, and any requirements for final delivery early. You can handle parts of the work in-house if everyone agrees on the handoff.

title: Corporate video production, from brief to final cut
description: A practical look at how a corporate video comes together and what your team should prepare.
cta: Share who the video needs to reach, where it will run, and when you need it.
sections: Start with one audience

A recruiting film, a customer story, and an internal launch can all feature the same office, but each has a different job. Write down who’s watching and what you want them to understand or do. That sentence will help when the team has to choose between two good ideas.
Find something the camera can show

If the message is that your team makes onboarding easy, show a real handoff or walk through what a customer sees on day one. Give interviewees prompts ahead of time so they can think of specific examples. Leave space for them to talk in their own words.
Make the shoot easy for your staff

Book a quiet room, let the crew know how to get in, and tell each participant how much time to hold. Identify any screens, badges, customer information, or areas that should stay out of frame. Share a contact who can handle questions during the shoot.
Review the story before the polish

On the first cut, check the message, accuracy, and pacing. Send consolidated notes with timestamps. Once the structure is approved, review names, graphics, captions, and the final files in the place they’ll actually be shown.
imageAlt: Tee Sama directing a corporate interview with a Blackmagic URSA Mini Pro

title: What type of corporate video does your business need?
description: Choose between a brand film, customer story, product demo, and recruiting video based on the job it needs to do.
cta: Choose a format for your goal
Tell us what your audience needs to see or understand. We can help you pick a format and scope the shoot.
sections: Brand film for an introduction

Use a brand film when people need to understand who you are and how you work. Give the viewer a scene they can remember. For a manufacturing business, a close look at a team solving a problem on the floor can tell you more than a montage of the building.
Customer story for a buying decision

If prospects are asking whether your service works for a business like theirs, find a customer who can talk about a specific before and after. Ask what triggered the decision and what changed day to day. A detail the customer remembers is more persuasive than a string of adjectives.
Product demo for a specific question

Show the action the viewer wants to understand. If there are three steps, film them clearly and in sequence. For a recruiting video, the equivalent is showing what a workday looks like and letting an employee explain what new hires can expect.
Choose the first place it will run

A homepage visitor, a sales prospect opening an email, and a candidate scrolling on a phone all arrive with different context. Pick the first placement before you write. It will help you decide what to show in the opening and what the viewer should do next.
imageAlt: A workshop supervisor demonstrating a product component to a colleague

title: What deliverables should you ask for on a corporate video shoot?
description: Plan the main edit, shorter versions, captions, and files your team will need after production.
cta: Share your publishing channels and launch dates. We can build a shoot plan that covers the edits you’ll use.
sections: Give each edit a purpose

The homepage film can explain the story in full. A short sales clip might answer one common objection. A vertical clip may have one good line and a clear next step. List what each version needs to do so the crew can capture the right opening and ending.
Plan framing while the camera is out

Some wide shots crop to vertical with no trouble. Two people sitting at opposite ends of a frame usually need another setup. Tell the crew early if a key demo or interview will need a vertical version so they can frame for it on set.
Get specific about captions and files

Ask for the formats your team can publish, including separate caption files or versions with captions built in. Check whether you need a clean version for an event, an alternate end card, or an archive master. Ask about raw footage separately if your internal team plans to edit later.
Use a one-page delivery list

Write one row per asset with the platform, length, aspect ratio, captions, and due date. Share it with whoever approves the video and whoever uploads it. That way a missing vertical cut is easier to catch before the crew wraps.
imageAlt: Tee Sama reviewing video edits at a workstation

title: How to hire an event videographer for a conference
description: What to ask before booking video coverage for a conference, panel, or company event.
cta: Send the date, venue, run of show, and the moments you can’t repeat. We can talk through crew and delivery.
sections: Decide what you’ll do with the footage

A recap for next year’s registration page and full recordings for attendees are two different jobs. Say which sessions you need in full, what belongs in the highlight edit, and whether sponsors need their own assets.
Walk through the schedule together

Mark moments that happen once and sessions that overlap. If a keynote and an interview are on opposite sides of the building at the same time, you’ll need a plan for both. Share load-in, access, and the name of a person who can relay changes.
Ask about audio

For a panel, ask how the videographer will work with the venue’s audio team and what backup they plan to record. For short interviews, pick a quiet spot nearby. A hallway looks convenient until the audience starts coming through.
Confirm delivery before booking

If you need a quick recap, agree on what goes into it and who can approve it on the day. Ask for a sample close to your event. Watch how the team moves between stage footage, interviews, and the audience, and listen for clarity.
imageAlt: Tee Sama operating a Blackmagic URSA Mini Pro at a conference

title: Event video recap or full recording? What to book
description: How to choose the right event video coverage for attendees, sponsors, and the next event.
cta: Tell us which sessions need to be recorded and who needs the footage afterward.
sections: Book a recap when you need the feeling of the room

A recap combines a few strong moments with reactions, location details, and short pieces of speech or interview. Give the crew one reason the event matters. That helps them find moments with a story instead of shooting every table and sign.
Book full recordings when the talks are the asset

If people will watch a session later, plan for steady coverage and clean audio throughout. Ask whether slides should appear in the final file and how audience questions will be recorded. Confirm which sessions need coverage if they run at the same time.
Give sponsor clips their own plan

Decide what each partner should receive and when. If a sponsor needs a short interview or a look at an activation, give the crew time and a point of contact. Check name spelling and sponsor marks before the event so the edit can move quickly.
Set two deadlines if you need speed and depth
You might need a short recap the next morning and longer edits later. Choose the handful of shots and quotes that must make the quick cut. Give the longer work its own review schedule.

title: How much does a corporate video cost?
description: What changes a corporate video quote, with examples of how to scope a project before you ask for pricing.
cta: Use the calculator for a starting range, then share your timeline and deliverables for a tailored estimate.
sections: Start with the project you can describe

A one-location customer interview with a short edit has a different scope from a campaign with three sites and several versions. Write down what you want to film and what you need at delivery. If you know when the final files are due, include that too.

For a starting point, Film Stop lists commercial production at $2,500 to $10,000+. That is our published range for commercials, and a corporate project can land at a different number depending on the brief. The calculator lets you change the scope before you ask for a tailored quote.
Account for preparation and production

A straightforward interview may need a short planning call and location check. A scripted shoot can require a treatment, casting, or more time to set up. Each company quotes differently, so ask who handles those items and whether the proposal includes them.
Look at the edit as its own cost

Captioning, custom graphics, music, and extra versions can all take time after the shoot. Ask whether shorter edits are separate cuts or trims of the master. If several people must approve the project, agree on revision rounds and who will send the notes.
Ask what you can simplify

Keep the people and scenes that tell the story. If you need to cut scope, see whether you can film at one location or deliver the main edit first. Use an estimate to compare those choices, then ask the producer what fits your brief.
imageAlt: A calculator and budget worksheet on a producer’s desk

title: How to budget for a one-day corporate video shoot
description: Build a budget around what can realistically fit in a day and what the editor needs afterward.
cta: Share your location, interview count, and edit list so we can estimate the crew and post-production.
sections: Count setups before you count interviews

Three interviews in the same quiet room can be straightforward. The same three people across two buildings add travel, resets, and fresh sound checks. List every room or look you need and how long each person is available.
Put must-have footage on the schedule first

For a customer story, protect the main interview and one scene that shows what the customer is describing. Add supporting footage if the timing works. If you need a product demo, block time to reset it and capture details from a second angle.
Budget the work after everyone goes home

Include the rough cut, reviews, audio, color, captions, and delivery. Decide whether the same footage will support social edits. Give each extra cut a clear purpose and confirm the producer included it in the estimate.
Ask for a base scope and options

A base scope could cover a single location, interviews, and one final edit. Ask for separate options for another setup or an extra cut. You’ll be able to see where the money goes and decide which additions are worth paying for.
